title: If you will (Mark 1:40–45)
hook: a man with leprosy says if you are willing; Jesus, moved, touches him

segments.voice: Yesterday: a mother-in-law and a whole town, and prayer a great while before day. Your line was a great while before day. Did you rise a little early? Day one hundred sixty-two.

A handshake, a hug, a hand on a shoulder: small touches nobody counts until they stop. For the man in today's story, they had stopped. He had a skin disease the Bible calls leprosy, and the law said he had to live outside the town, clothes torn, calling out a warning so nobody came near. Nobody touched him. Nobody was supposed to. And one day, breaking every rule of distance, he walks straight up to Jesus and kneels. Today's word is what everyone called him.
screen: `NO HANDSHAKE, NO HUG.` → `OUTSIDE THE TOWN, CALLING A WARNING.` → `HE KNEELS IN FRONT OF JESUS.`

segments.voice: Leper. It's the old word for a person with leprosy. Today some people prefer to say a person with leprosy, because a leper came to mean an outcast, and that's exactly what this man was. In the Bible, leprosy covers a range of skin diseases, not only what doctors now call Hansen's disease. The book of Leviticus says such a person "shall cry, Unclean, unclean," and "he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his habitation be." Alone. Outside. Now listen to how he asks, in the King James Bible: "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Not can you. He's sure Jesus can. His question is whether Jesus wants to. If you are willing. That's the question underneath a lot of human pain: not is it possible, but does anyone want to? Then Mark: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean." I will. I am willing. And before a word of healing, a touch. It comes while he is still unclean, by the law's own terms. Under the purity laws, uncleanness could pass by touch. Mark tells it the other way round: Jesus touches, and the man is made clean. A scholar's detail: a few old manuscripts say not moved with compassion, but moved with anger. Anger at what? At the disease, perhaps, or at his isolation. Scholars still debate which reading is original. Then a twist. Jesus tells the man to tell no one, and to show himself to the priest as the law required. The man tells everyone. And now Jesus can't openly enter a town. He has to stay out in the lonely places. The outsider comes in, and Jesus ends up outside.
screen: `OUTSIDE THE CAMP, ALONE.` · `NOT CAN YOU, BUT DO YOU WANT TO.` · `A TOUCH BEFORE A WORD.` · `THE OUTSIDER IN, JESUS OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `I WILL; BE THOU CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Rest one hand on your own shoulder, or over your heart, and just notice what a kind touch feels like. Then think of someone who may not have been touched kindly in a while. An older neighbor. A friend living alone. Someone grieving. Someone everyone seems to keep at a distance. Hold their face for a minute. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well. Then think of one appropriate, kind touch you could offer: a handshake, a hug, a hand on a shoulder. The bell holds the time.
Leper. A person with a skin disease who, by law, lived alone outside the town. Jesus touched him first.
Your line: I am willing. Today, offer someone a kind, welcome touch: a hand on a shoulder, a real handshake, a hug. Day one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Many Christians take this story as a call to reach people who are isolated, and Christian groups have long run hospitals and missions for people with leprosy and other stigmatized illnesses.

fork.setup: a man with leprosy kneels in front of you, against every rule of distance, and says: if you are willing, you can make me clean. what does Jesus do?

fork.reveal: "put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean." the touch came first, while the man was still unclean.

original.note: Greek: I will, be made clean — Jesus's answer (Mark 1:41).

trapdoor: what you thought: a leper is a word for an outcast.
what it means: a man who lived alone by law, asking not if Jesus could, but if he wanted to, and touched before he was healed.
what a scholar hears: most manuscripts read splanchnistheis, moved with compassion; a few, including Codex Bezae, read orgistheis, moved with anger. the debate over which is original continues.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook rewritten (opened 'Think about' and 'Now imagine', told the listener what they'd felt); uncited 'in years' cut; the purity-law line reworded so the law is described, not used as a foil.
The index carry 'I am willing' paraphrases the KJV 'I will' (θέλω); the voice ties them together. Confirm.
Biblical tsara'at / Greek lepra covering various skin conditions, not necessarily Hansen's disease: confirm.
Language note: 'person with leprosy' preferred today; the index word 'leper' is kept as required. Confirm handling.
Textual variant: ὀργισθείς (moved with anger) in Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin witnesses vs σπλαγχνισθείς. Confirm.
Touching someone with tsara'at conveying impurity under the law: confirm phrasing ('By the law, touching made you unclean too').
Practice invites an 'appropriate, kind touch'; please check it is sensitive to people who don't welcome touch.

'Here, the cleanness goes the other way' and 'By the law, touching made you unclean too': check this does not frame Levitical purity law (ritual, not moral, impurity) as something Jesus overturns in a way that disparages Jewish practice. Jesus also sends the man to the priest as the law required, which the script mentions.
